claim: CCN1 (CYR61) stimulates active angiogenesis in various tumours.
source: CCN1 (CYR61) stimulates active angiogenesis in various tumours, although the mechanism is largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact, though the mechanism is noted as largely unknown.

claim: CCN1 is a key regulator of endothelial tip cell activity in angiogenesis.
source: Here, we report that CCN1 is a key regulator of endothelial tip cell activity in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Microvessel networks and directional vascular cell migration patterns were deformed in ccn1-knockdown zebrafish embryos.
source: Microvessel networks and directional vascular cell migration patterns were deformed in ccn1-knockdown zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in zebrafish embryos as shown in Figure 1.

claim: CCN1 activated VEGFR2 and downstream MAPK/PI3K signalling pathways.
source: CCN1 activated VEGFR2 and downstream MAPK/PI3K signalling pathways, YAP/TAZ, as well as Rho effector mDia1 to enhance tip cell activity and CCN1 itself.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and other experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CCN1 activated YAP/TAZ to enhance tip cell activity.
source: CCN1 activated VEGFR2 and downstream MAPK/PI3K signalling pathways, YAP/TAZ, as well as Rho effector mDia1 to enhance tip cell activity and CCN1 itself.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data showing YAP/TAZ nuclear localization and phosphorylation changes in Figure 3.

claim: CCN1 activated Rho effector mDia1 to enhance tip cell activity.
source: CCN1 activated VEGFR2 and downstream MAPK/PI3K signalling pathways, YAP/TAZ, as well as Rho effector mDia1 to enhance tip cell activity and CCN1 itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing mDia1 involvement in filopodial formation.

claim: VEGFR2 interacted with integrin αvβ3 through CCN1.
source: VEGFR2 interacted with integrin αvβ3 through CCN1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Integrin αvβ3 inhibitor repressed tip cell number and sprouting in postnatal retinas from endothelial cell-specific Ccn1 transgenic mice.
source: Integrin αvβ3 inhibitor repressed tip cell number and sprouting in postnatal retinas from endothelial cell-specific Ccn1 transgenic mice, and allograft tumours in Ccn1 transgenic mice showed hyperactive vascular sprouting.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from retinal analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Allograft tumours in Ccn1 transgenic mice showed hyperactive vascular sprouting.
source: Integrin αvβ3 inhibitor repressed tip cell number and sprouting in postnatal retinas from endothelial cell-specific Ccn1 transgenic mice, and allograft tumours in Ccn1 transgenic mice showed hyperactive vascular sprouting.
evidence: This is supported by tumor allograft data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cancer patients with high CCN1 expression have poor survival outcomes.
source: Cancer patients with high CCN1 expression have poor survival outcomes and positive correlation with ITGAV and ITGB3 and high YAP/WWTR1.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cancer patients with high CCN1 expression show positive correlation with ITGAV and ITGB3.
source: Cancer patients with high CCN1 expression have poor survival outcomes and positive correlation with ITGAV and ITGB3 and high YAP/WWTR1.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cancer patients with high CCN1 expression show high YAP/WWTR1.
source: Cancer patients with high CCN1 expression have poor survival outcomes and positive correlation with ITGAV and ITGB3 and high YAP/WWTR1.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: CCN1 regulates tip cell activity through positive feedback regulation via integrin αvβ3/VEGFR2 and increased YAP/TAZ activity.
source: Thus, our data underscore the positive feedback regulation of tip cells by CCN1 through integrin αvβ3/VEGFR2 and increased YAP/TAZ activity, suggesting a promising therapeutic intervention for pathological angiogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ECM is important for dynamic and multifunctional regulation of cell behaviours.
source: The ECM is important for dynamic and multifunctional regulation of cell behaviours and can modulate the bioavailability and activity of growth factors, cytokines, and extracellular enzymes (Aszódi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aszódi et al., 2006.

claim: ECM proteins directly interact with cell surface receptors to activate signal transduction.
source: In addition, ECM proteins directly interact with cell surface receptors to activate signal transduction (Bornstein and Sage, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bornstein and Sage, 2002.

claim: CCN1 is a secreted protein that is a target of the YAP/TAZ Hippo signalling molecules.
source: Within the CCN protein family, cysteine-rich angiogenic inducer 61 (CYR61, also known as CCN1) is a secreted protein that is a target of the YAP/TAZ Hippo signalling molecules (Zhang et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Yu et al., 2012.

claim: CCN1 mediates a variety of cellular processes, including adhesion, chemotaxis stimulation, survival, and angiogenesis, in a cell type-dependent manner.
source: CCN1 has been reported to mediate a variety of cellular processes, including adhesion, chemotaxis stimulation, survival, and angiogenesis, in a cell type-dependent manner (Grzeszkiewicz et al., 2002; Lin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grzeszkiewicz et al., 2002 and Lin et al., 2004.

claim: CCN1 regulates the expression and activities of angiogenic factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), in fibroblasts and osteoblasts.
source: CCN1 also regulates the expression and activities of angiogenic factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), in fibroblasts and osteoblasts (Chen et al., 2001; Ivkovic et al., 2003; Athanasopoulos et al., 2007; Dean et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001; Ivkovic et al., 2003; Athanasopoulos et al., 2007; Dean et al., 2007.

claim: CCN1 is required for re-endothelialisation and wound repair in contexts where angiogenesis is indispensable.
source: It is required for re-endothelialisation and wound repair in contexts where angiogenesis is indispensable (Athanasopoulos et al., 2007; Bär et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Athanasopoulos et al., 2007 and Bär et al., 2010.

claim: The angiogenic behaviour of CCN1 has been attributed to its binding to integrin αvβ3.
source: The angiogenic behaviour of CCN1 has been attributed to its binding to integrin αvβ3, a major integrin expressed in ECs (Leu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leu et al., 2002.

claim: Ccn1-null mice suffer embryonic lethality due to insufficient placental and embryonic blood vessel integrity.
source: Ccn1-null mice suffer embryonic lethality due to insufficient placental and embryonic blood vessel integrity (Babic et al., 1998), and Ccn1-knockdown in mouse embryos causes atrioventricular valve and septal defects due to apoptosis in the cushion tissue and reduction in gelatinase activity (Mo and Lau, 2006); this phenotype overlaps with VEGF-knockout phenotypes in the cardiovascular system (Dor et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Babic et al., 1998; Mo and Lau, 2006; Dor et al., 2001.

claim: CCN1 is not expressed much in ECs but is rather expressed in other parenchymal or mesenchymal cells.
source: However, CCN1 is not expressed much in ECs but is rather expressed in other parenchymal or mesenchymal cells (Su et al., 2004), and thus, an EC-specific knockout strategy is likely not suitable for identification of the role of CCN1 in sprouting angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Su et al., 2004.

claim: YAP/TAZ are overexpressed in various cancer tissues and have been identified as prognostic markers.
source: YAP/TAZ are overexpressed in various cancer tissues and have been identified as prognostic markers (Wang et al., 2013; Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2013 and Han et al., 2014.

claim: IHC of tumours has revealed prominent expression and nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ in correlation with malignant features and poor patient outcomes.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) of tumours has revealed prominent expression and nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ in correlation with malignant features and poor patient outcomes (Zanconato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zanconato et al., 2016.

claim: CCN1 is a well-known transcriptional target of YAP/TAZ.
source: CCN1 is a well-known transcriptional target of YAP/TAZ (Zhao et al., 2008), is secreted in cancer cells, and induces extensive tumour angiogenesis, underscoring its paracrine angiogenic effect (Harris et al., 2012; Maity et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2008; Harris et al., 2012; Maity et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of YAP/TAZ by VEGF facilitates expression of CCN1.
source: In addition, activation of YAP/TAZ by VEGF, a known angiogenic factor, facilitates expression of CCN1 (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: YAP is present in embryonic retinal vessels.
source: The presence of YAP in embryonic retinal vessels, along with reduced retinal vascular sprouting and decreased numbers of vascular branches upon EC-specific deletion of embryonic YAP/TAZ, has further emphasised the importance of YAP/TAZ in vascular development (Choi and Kwon, 2015; Sakabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi and Kwon, 2015 and Sakabe et al., 2017.

claim: EC-specific deletion of embryonic YAP/TAZ results in reduced retinal vascular sprouting and decreased numbers of vascular branches.
source: The presence of YAP in embryonic retinal vessels, along with reduced retinal vascular sprouting and decreased numbers of vascular branches upon EC-specific deletion of embryonic YAP/TAZ, has further emphasised the importance of YAP/TAZ in vascular development (Choi and Kwon, 2015; Sakabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi and Kwon, 2015 and Sakabe et al., 2017.

claim: Tip cells are characterised by their position at the very tops of angiogenic sprouts and have extensive filopodial protrusions directed toward angiogenic attractants.
source: Tip cells are characterised by their position at the very tops of angiogenic sprouts and have extensive filopodial protrusions directed toward angiogenic attractants.
evidence: This is a description of tip cell characteristics based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tip cells have a specific molecular signature, characterised by the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2), VEGFR3, and DLL4.
source: Tip cells have a specific molecular signature, characterised by the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2), VEGFR3, and DLL4.
evidence: This is a description of tip cell molecular markers based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The VEGF gradient is important in the selection and induction of endothelial tip cells.
source: It has been reported that the VEGF gradient is important in the selection and induction of endothelial tip cells.
evidence: This is stated as a reported finding in the field.

claim: Binding of VEGFR2 induces a signalling cascade that enables the activation of Notch-Delta signalling via DLL4 expression in ECs, converting them into tip cells.
source: Binding of VEGFR2 induces a signalling cascade that enables the activation of Notch-Delta signalling via DLL4 expression in ECs, converting them into tip cells; however, mechanism of sustained tip cell activity other than VEGF-mediated signalling has not yet been elucidated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with the caveat that sustained tip cell activity mechanisms are not fully understood.

claim: MO-mediated knockdown of ccn1 caused the formation of small heads, oedema, and bent trunk regions in zebrafish embryos.
source: MO-mediated knockdown of ccn1 caused the formation of small heads, oedema, and bent trunk regions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by observations in zebrafish embryos shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In ccn1 morphants, the vasculature in the head and trunk regions was abnormally sprouted and disconnected.
source: In TG (flk1:EGFP) embryos, control MO injection resulted in the formation of T-shaped intersegmental vessels (ISVs) and dorsolateral anastomose vessels (DLAVs) at 40 hr post-fertilisation (hpf) (I′ and II′ in Figure 1B), whereas the vasculature in the head and trunk regions of ccn1 morphants was abnormally sprouted and disconnected (III′, IV′, V′, and VI′ in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging of zebrafish embryos shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ccn1 morphants lost the T-shaped morphology previously displayed at the DLAV and ISV connexions.
source: ccn1 morphants lost the T-shaped morphology previously displayed at the DLAV and ISV connexions (IV′ and VI′ in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging of zebrafish embryos shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In ccn1 morphants, frontal cells from the DA took a right and then left-ascending or bifurcating path to DLAV or did not migrate from DAV.
source: When we observed more precisely in ISVs, in control animals, frontal cells from the DA migrated along a left-ascending path to the parachordal vessel (PAV) and then along a right-ascending path to the DLAV (I and II, arrows in Figure 1B); conversely, in two kinds of ccn1 morphants, these cells took a right and then left-ascending or bifurcating path to DLAV or not migrating from DAV (III-VI, arrows in Figure 1C, Figure 1D), and disconnected or malformed DLAV (III-VI arrowheads in Figure 1C, Figure 1D) were significantly increased at both 32 and 40 hpf.
evidence: This is supported by detailed imaging and quantification shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Injection of sense RNA of ccn1 significantly rescued the vascular malformations and altered phenotypes induced by ccn1 morpholinos.
source: However, injection of sense RNA of ccn1 significantly rescued the vascular malformations and altered phenotypes induced by ccn1 morpholinos (Figure 1C VII and VIII), suggesting that CCN1 is an essential factor for the vascular development in zebrafish.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ccn1 morphants demonstrated ectopic expression of flk-1, which was expressed not in vascular ECs but across the entire anterior–posterior body axis.
source: In addition, ccn1 morphants demonstrated ectopic expression of flk-1, which was expressed not in vascular ECs but across the entire anterior–posterior body axis (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In ccn1 morphants, aortic vessels disappeared and changed into venous types as detected by in situ expression of Notch-1b (aortic marker) and Flt-4 (venous marker).
source: Aortic vessels disappeared and changed into venous types as detected by in situ expression of Notch-1b (aortic marker) and Flt-4 (venous marker) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCN1 induced intensive vascular sprouts from aortic explants.
source: CCN1 induced intensive vascular sprouts from aortic explants and significantly increased tip cell populations to the same degree as VEGF, as determined by tip cell markers, DLL4 and CD34 (Siemerink et al., 2012) as well as an EC marker, CD31 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by aortic ring assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CCN1 significantly increased tip cell populations to the same degree as VEGF in aortic explants.
source: CCN1 induced intensive vascular sprouts from aortic explants and significantly increased tip cell populations to the same degree as VEGF, as determined by tip cell markers, DLL4 and CD34 (Siemerink et al., 2012) as well as an EC marker, CD31 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of tip cells in aortic ring assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CCN1 significantly increased sprouting branches from spheroids.
source: CCN1 also significantly increased sprouting branches from spheroids, as determined by both lengths and numbers of tip cells after immunostained with DLL4 and CD34 antibodies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by spheroid sprouting assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Filopodia markedly increased upon exposure to CCN1 in human ECs.
source: Filopodial formation, which is an important marker of tip cells in migrating cells, was also detected in vitro by immunostaining with phalloidin. In human ECs, filopodia markedly increased upon exposure to CCN1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CCN1 markedly increased capillary tube formation.
source: CCN1 markedly increased capillary tube formation (Figure 2D) and promoted EC migration in the wound migration assay (Figure 2E, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by tube formation assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CCN1 promoted EC migration in the wound migration assay.
source: CCN1 markedly increased capillary tube formation (Figure 2D) and promoted EC migration in the wound migration assay (Figure 2E, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by wound migration assay data shown in Figure 2E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Expression levels of tip cell marker genes like VEGFR2, DLL4, and SOX17 were elevated by CCN1.
source: Expression levels of tip cell marker genes like VEGFR2, DLL4 (Hellström et al., 2007), and SOX17 (Lee et al., 2014) were elevated, but those of stalk cell marker genes like JAG1, ROBO4, and NOTCH1 were not changed by CCN1, nor by VEGF (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Stalk cell marker genes like JAG1, ROBO4, and NOTCH1 were not changed by CCN1.
source: Expression levels of tip cell marker genes like VEGFR2, DLL4 (Hellström et al., 2007), and SOX17 (Lee et al., 2014) were elevated, but those of stalk cell marker genes like JAG1, ROBO4, and NOTCH1 were not changed by CCN1, nor by VEGF (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Protein levels of VEGFR2, DLL4, and SOX17 were increased by CCN1.
source: Protein levels of VEGFR2, DLL4, and SOX17 were also increased by CCN1 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: DLL4-Luc reporter activity was significantly increased by CCN1.
source: To confirm these results, DLL4 promoter-driven luciferase (DLL4-Luc) reporter activity was observed. DLL4-Luc reporter activity was significantly increased by CCN1, as by VEGF (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: YAP and TAZ translocation to the nucleus was significantly upregulated by treatment with CCN1 for 1 hr in a dose-dependent manner.
source: YAP and TAZ translocation to the nucleus was significantly upregulated by treatment with CCN1 for 1 hr in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated LATS were decreased maximally at 1 hr by CCN1 in HUVECs.
source: We found that levels of phosphorylated LATS were decreased maximally at 1 hr and those of phosphorylated YAP/TAZ were decreased from 15 min, maximally at 1 hr by CCN1 in HUVECs (Figure 3B), indicating that CCN1 activates YAP/TAZ in ECs at the early time after stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated YAP/TAZ were decreased from 15 min, maximally at 1 hr by CCN1 in HUVECs.
source: We found that levels of phosphorylated LATS were decreased maximally at 1 hr and those of phosphorylated YAP/TAZ were decreased from 15 min, maximally at 1 hr by CCN1 in HUVECs (Figure 3B), indicating that CCN1 activates YAP/TAZ in ECs at the early time after stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CCN1 induced the phosphorylation of VEGFR2 from 10 min.
source: CCN1 induced the phosphorylation of VEGFR2 from 10 min at slightly earlier time point of YAP/TAZ activation within 1 hr (Figure 3C) and in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CCN1 induced the phosphorylation of VEGFR2 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: CCN1 induced the phosphorylation of VEGFR2 from 10 min at slightly earlier time point of YAP/TAZ activation within 1 hr (Figure 3C) and in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: VEGFR2 activation after serum stimulation was highly repressed upon siRNA-mediated CCN1 knockdown.
source: VEGFR2 activation after serum stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Latinkic et al., 2001) was highly repressed upon siRNA-mediated CCN1 knockdown (siCCN1) (Figure 3E), suggesting that CCN1 activates VEGFR2.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CCN1 activated VEGFR2 regardless of endogenous VEGF.
source: To confirm whether CCN1 is able to activate VEGFR2 in the absence of endogenous VEGF, we transfected HUVECs with siVEGF and found that CCN1 activated VEGFR2 regardless of endogenous VEGF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of CCN1 with siCCN1 repressed the mRNA expression of the tip cells markers, DLL4 and VEGFR2.
source: Knockdown of CCN1 with siCCN1 repressed the mRNA expression of the tip cells markers, DLL4 and VEGFR2 (Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) as well as the migration and sprouting ability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), indicating that endothelial CCN1 is important for EC tip cell activity.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knockdown of CCN1 with siCCN1 repressed the migration and sprouting ability of ECs.
source: Knockdown of CCN1 with siCCN1 repressed the mRNA expression of the tip cells markers, DLL4 and VEGFR2 (Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) as well as the migration and sprouting ability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), indicating that endothelial CCN1 is important for EC tip cell activity.
evidence: This is supported by spheroid assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ERK, p38 MAPK, and p85 PI3K were activated by CCN1.
source: Therefore, we checked that extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), p38 MAPK, and p85 PI3K, all downstream targets of Y1175 phosphorylation, were activated by CCN1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: DLL4 mRNA and protein levels were highly repressed upon treatment with MAPK and PI3K inhibitors except SP600125.
source: Next, to confirm whether CCN1-mediated tip cell activity involves the MAPK and PI3K signalling cascades, we used pharmacological inhibitors for ERK1/2 (PD98059), p38 MAPK (SB203580), JNK MAPK (SP600125), and PI3K (LY294002). Upon treatment with all inhibitors except SP600125, DLL4 mRNA and protein levels were highly repressed (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Filopodial formation was highly reduced in ECs exposed to CCN1 together with MAPK and PI3K inhibitors.
source: To confirm these results, filopodial formation, as determined by phalloidin staining, was highly reduced in ECs exposed to CCN1 together with the inhibitors (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CCN1 increased the phosphorylation of STAT-1 and STAT-3.
source: CCN1-mediated increases in the phosphorylation of STAT-1 and STAT-3 further implicate its probable involvement in VEGFR2 activation, similar to that of VEGF (Bartoli et al., 2000; Bartoli et al., 2003) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The phosphorylation of LATS1 and YAP/TAZ was decreased by CCN1, but the PD98059, SB203580, and LY294002 inhibitors restored phosphorylation to control levels.
source: The phosphorylation of LATS1 and YAP/TAZ was decreased by CCN1, but the PD98059, SB203580, and LY294002 inhibitors restored phosphorylation to control levels, thus confirming the repression of phosphorylated LATS1 in ECs, resulting in YAP/TAZ activation by CCN1 (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Expression of YAP/TAZ target gene CCN1 was significantly increased by CCN1 treatment and repressed by PD98059, SB203580, and LY294002.
source: In support of these findings, expression of YAP/TAZ target gene CCN1 was also significantly increased by CCN1 treatment and repressed by PD98059, SB203580, and LY294002 (Figure 3K), suggesting the involvement of MAPK and PI3K as well as the expression of CCN1 via the activation of YAP/TAZ in ECs.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Verteporfin inhibited VEGFR2, CCN1, and DLL4 expression induced by CCN1.
source: An inhibitor of YAP/TAZ, verteporfin (VP), inhibited VEGFR2, CCN1, and DLL4 expression induced by CCN1, confirming the involvement of YAP/TAZ in tip cell activity (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: CCN1 increased DIAPH1 mRNA expression by 1.5-fold.
source: We found that CCN1 increased DIAPH1 mRNA expression by 1.5-fold (Figure 4A) and also overexpression of DIAPH1 (mDia1) increased filopodial numbers similar to that in CCN1-treated HUVECs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of DIAPH1 (mDia1) increased filopodial numbers similar to that in CCN1-treated HUVECs.
source: We found that CCN1 increased DIAPH1 mRNA expression by 1.5-fold (Figure 4A) and also overexpression of DIAPH1 (mDia1) increased filopodial numbers similar to that in CCN1-treated HUVECs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DIAPH1 dominant-negative mutation decreased CCN1-induced filopodial formation.
source: However, DIAPH1 dominant-negative mutation decreased CCN1-induced filopodial formation (Figure 4B), suggesting that mDia1 is essential for CCN1-induced filopodial formation in ECs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The active form of Cdc42 was increased by CCN1 treatment and DIAPH1 overexpression but not the DIAPH1 mutant with CCN1.
source: The active form of Cdc42 assayed by pull-down and immunoprecipitation (IP) analysis as described previously (Wang et al., 2003) was increased by CCN1 treatment and DIAPH1 overexpression but not the DIAPH1 mutant with CCN1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Cdc42 pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Phosphorylated N-Wasp was detected in CCN1-treated and DIAPH1-overexpressing cells but not in DIAPH1 mutant-expressing cells.
source: Phosphorylated N-Wasp, induced by active Cdc42 (Sakabe et al., 2017), was also detected in CCN1-treated and DIAPH1-overexpressing cells but not in DIAPH1 mutant-expressing cells (Figure 4D), suggesting that mDia1 is required for CCN1-induced Cdc42 activation in tip cell formation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ was induced by overexpression of DIAPH1 as well as CCN1 treatment, but not by the DIAPH1 DN mutants.
source: Nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ was induced by overexpression of DIAPH1 as well as CCN1 treatment, but not by the DIAPH1 DN mutants (Figure 4E), indicating that mDia1 is necessary for YAP/TAZ nuclear translocation in CCN1-induced tip cell formation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CCN1 increased β3 integrin expression.
source: CCN1, as well as VEGF increased β3 integrin expression according to western blotting (WB) and immunofluorescence (IF) assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), suggesting autocrine regulation of CCN1 angiogenic signalling through integrin αvβ3.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: IP and WB analyses showed strong interactions between VEGFR2 and integrin αvβ3, as well as their interaction with CCN1 upon CCN1 treatment for 24 hr.
source: IP and WB analyses showed strong interactions between VEGFR2 and integrin αvβ3, as well as their interaction with CCN1 upon CCN1 treatment for 24 hr. However, cell exposure to the αvβ3 inhibitor peptide cyclo(RGDfK) blocked the interactions of VEGFR2 with integrin αvβ3, CCN1 with integrin αvβ3, and CCN1 with VEGFR2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cell exposure to the αvβ3 inhibitor peptide cyclo(RGDfK) blocked the interactions of VEGFR2 with integrin αvβ3, CCN1 with integrin αvβ3, and CCN1 with VEGFR2.
source: IP and WB analyses showed strong interactions between VEGFR2 and integrin αvβ3, as well as their interaction with CCN1 upon CCN1 treatment for 24 hr. However, cell exposure to the αvβ3 inhibitor peptide cyclo(RGDfK) blocked the interactions of VEGFR2 with integrin αvβ3, CCN1 with integrin αvβ3, and CCN1 with VEGFR2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In situ PLA revealed increased interactions among CCN1/integrin αvβ3/VEGFR2 in ECs compared to that in controls.
source: In addition, in situ proximity ligation assay (PLA) also clearly revealed increased interactions among CCN1/integrin αvβ3/VEGFR2 in ECs compared to that in controls (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CCN1-induced VEGFR2 downstream kinase signalling activity was inhibited by cyclo(RGDfK).
source: CCN1-induced VEGFR2 downstream kinase signalling activity was inhibited by cyclo(RGDfK) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Co-treatment with cyclo(RGDfK) rescued the decreased phosphorylation of YAP/TAZ by CCN1.
source: We also determined whether integrin αvβ3 is essential for YAP/TAZ activation by CCN1. Co-treatment with cyclo(RGDfK) rescued the decreased phosphorylation of YAP/TAZ by CCN1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Increased YAP/TAZ nuclear localization in the CCN1-treated group was blocked by cyclo(RGDfK) co-treatment.
source: At the same time, increased YAP/TAZ nuclear localization in the CCN1-treated group was blocked by cyclo(RGDfK) co-treatment (Figure 5E), followed by repressed DLL4-Luc activity and expression of tip cell marker genes DLL4 and SOX17 (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5E.

claim: cyclo(RGDfK) co-treatment repressed DLL4-Luc activity and expression of tip cell marker genes DLL4 and SOX17.
source: At the same time, increased YAP/TAZ nuclear localization in the CCN1-treated group was blocked by cyclo(RGDfK) co-treatment (Figure 5E), followed by repressed DLL4-Luc activity and expression of tip cell marker genes DLL4 and SOX17 (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: In aortas treated with cyclo(RGDfK), CCN1-induced tip cell numbers were significantly decreased.
source: We then repeated the aortic ring and EC spheroid sprouting assays in the presence of cyclo(RGDfK). In aortas treated with cyclo(RGDfK), CCN1-induced tip cell numbers were significantly decreased CD31+/DLL4+/CD34+ tip cells in Figure 5H.
evidence: This is supported by aortic ring assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: CCN1 increased the sprouting length and tip cell number by 2- and 3.5-fold, respectively, when compared to control group in cultured spheroids, and this was abolished by cyclo(RGDfK).
source: CCN1 increased the sprouting length and tip cell number by 2- and 3.5-fold, respectively, when compared to control group, and this was abolished by cyclo(RGDfK) in cultured spheroids (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by spheroid sprouting assay data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: CCN1 was not highly expressed in retinal ECs at postnatal day 6 (P6).
source: Visualisation of developing vessels by IF staining with isolectin B4 and CCN1 antibodies revealed that CCN1 was not highly expressed in retinal ECs at postnatal day 6 (P6) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Chintala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from Chintala et al., 2015.

claim: In EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice, CCN1 was expressed in retinal ECs.
source: In EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice, we confirmed that CCN1 was expressed in retinal ECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), together with significant increases in retinal vessel branching and number of tip cells with filopodia (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice showed significant increases in retinal vessel branching and number of tip cells with filopodia.
source: In EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice, we confirmed that CCN1 was expressed in retinal ECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), together with significant increases in retinal vessel branching and number of tip cells with filopodia (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by retinal vessel imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: In each retinal quadrant, the radial outgrowth of retinal vessels from the optic nerve head to the peripheral vascular front was similar to that observed in wild-type (WT) mice.
source: However, in each retinal quadrant, the radial outgrowth of retinal vessels from the optic nerve head to the peripheral vascular front was similar to that observed in wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 6A), indicating a specific role for CCN1 in endothelial branching and tip cell formation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by retinal vessel imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Following injection of cyclo(RGDfK) for 2 days, the number of sprouting tip cells with filopodia significantly decreased at P5 and P6.
source: Following injection of cyclo(RGDfK) for 2 days, the number of sprouting tip cells with filopodia significantly decreased at P5 and P6 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by retinal vessel imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The aortic rings isolated from Ccn1-TG mice showed an increased number of tip cells and sprouting ECs compared to those in WT mice, and these were significantly reduced in cyclo(RGDfK)-treated aortas.
source: The aortic rings isolated from these TG mice showed an increased number of tip cells and sprouting ECs compared to those in WT mice, and these were significantly reduced in cyclo(RGDfK)-treated aortas (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by aortic ring assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: cyclo(RGDfK) treatment repressed in vivo angiogenesis in the Matrigel plug assay.
source: In addition, cyclo(RGDfK) treatment repressed in vivo angiogenesis in the Matrigel plug assay. Haematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of sections of plugs from Ccn1-TG mice revealed an increased number of neovessels and microvessels compared to that in controls, while in Matrigel plugs treated with cyclo(RGDfK), both neovessel and microvessel densities were decreased compared to those in Ccn1-TG mice without cyclo(RGDfK) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by Matrigel plug assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Treatment with SU5416, a VEGFR2 kinase-specific inhibitor, demonstrated the same inhibitory results in CAM and Matrigel plug assays following treatment with CCN1.
source: We also confirmed that treatment with SU5416, a VEGFR2 kinase-specific inhibitor, demonstrated the same inhibitory results in CAM and Matrigel plug assays following treatment with CCN1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by CAM and Matrigel plug assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Levels of plasma VEGF did not differ between WT and EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice.
source: To rule out endogenous VEGF as a prime effector of angiogenesis in Ccn1-TG mice, we compared the plasma VEGF levels of the WT and TG mice. Levels of plasma VEGF did not differ between WT and EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice, and treatment of cultured ECs with CCN1 did not affect secreted VEGF levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Treatment of cultured ECs with CCN1 did not affect secreted VEGF levels.
source: To rule out endogenous VEGF as a prime effector of angiogenesis in Ccn1-TG mice, we compared the plasma VEGF levels of the WT and TG mice. Levels of plasma VEGF did not differ between WT and EC-specific Ccn1-TG mice, and treatment of cultured ECs with CCN1 did not affect secreted VEGF levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In Ccn1-TG mice, significantly increased and co-localised expression of VEGFR2 and integrin β3 was observed in the front region of the retinal vessels.
source: Finally, we confirmed the expression patterns of VEGFR2 and integrin β3 in the mice. In Ccn1-TG mice, we observed significantly increased and co-localised expression of VEGFR2 and integrin β3 in the front region of the retinal vessels (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Induced expression of Ccn1 in ECs induced active angiogenic vessels, representing a significant decrease in pericyte coverage, both in the central and peripheral regions of the tumour.
source: Surprisingly, induced expression of Ccn1 in ECs induced active angiogenic vessels, representing a significant decrease in pericyte coverage, both in the central and peripheral regions of the tumour (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of tumor sections shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ccn1 overexpression in ECs resulted in significant upregulation of VEGFR2 expression as well as increased sprouting activity in the central region of the tumour.
source: Ccn1 overexpression in ECs resulted in significant upregulation of VEGFR2 expression as well as increased sprouting activity in the central region of the tumour (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of tumor sections shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The overall survival rate was significantly higher in those with low expression of CCN1 compared to that in the high expression group among lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) patients.
source: The overall survival rate was significantly higher in those with low expression of CCN1 compared to that in the high expression group among lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) (Figure 7C) as well as bladder urothelial cancer (BLCA) and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) patients (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The overall survival rate was significantly higher in those with low expression of CCN1 compared to that in the high expression group among bladder urothelial cancer (BLCA) and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) patients.
source: The overall survival rate was significantly higher in those with low expression of CCN1 compared to that in the high expression group among lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) (Figure 7C) as well as bladder urothelial cancer (BLCA) and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) patients (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: CCN1 expression was significantly positively correlated with ITGB3, VEGFR2, DLL4, YAP and WWTR1 in LUSC.
source: In addition, we compared the expression of ITGB3, VEGFR2, DLL4, YAP and WWTR1 in the CCN1-low and -high groups. CCN1 expression was significantly positively correlated with ITGB3, VEGFR2, DLL4, YAP and WWTR1 in LUSC (Figure 7D), BLCA, and STAD (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by box plot analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: CCN1 expression was significantly positively correlated with ITGB3, VEGFR2, DLL4, YAP and WWTR1 in BLCA and STAD.
source: In addition, we compared the expression of ITGB3, VEGFR2, DLL4, YAP and WWTR1 in the CCN1-low and -high groups. CCN1 expression was significantly positively correlated with ITGB3, VEGFR2, DLL4, YAP and WWTR1 in LUSC (Figure 7D), BLCA, and STAD (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by box plot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: The expression of angiogenic factors including VEGFR2 and Tie2 is significantly correlated with the expression of CCN1 in LUSC, BLCA, and STAD cancer patient cohorts.
source: And the expression of angiogenic factors including VEGFR2 and Tie2 is significantly correlated with the expression of CCN1 in these cancer patient cohorts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Spearman's rank correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In BLCA, age and stage of cancer showed significant difference or enrichment between CCN1 high and CCN1 low patient groups.
source: However, age showed no significant difference between CCN1 high or CCN1 low patient group in LUSC and STAD cohorts, whereas, in BLCA, age and stage of cancer showed significant (p<0.05) difference or enrichment between CCN1 high and CCN1 low patient groups, suggesting potential association of age and stage of cancer with patient survival in BLCA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: Overexpression of YAP/TAZ increases CCN1 expression and secretion from cancer cells into the tumour microenvironment.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that overexpression of YAP/TAZ increases CCN1 expression and secretion from cancer cells into the tumour microenvironment, which activates tip cell activity by increasing the expression of YAP/TAZ as well as VEGFR2 and DLL4 in ECs to promote vascular sprouting and tumour angiogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of the study showing YAP/TAZ regulation of CCN1 and CCN1's effects on tip cells.

claim: CCN1 activates tip cell activity by increasing the expression of YAP/TAZ as well as VEGFR2 and DLL4 in ECs to promote vascular sprouting and tumour angiogenesis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that overexpression of YAP/TAZ increases CCN1 expression and secretion from cancer cells into the tumour microenvironment, which activates tip cell activity by increasing the expression of YAP/TAZ as well as VEGFR2 and DLL4 in ECs to promote vascular sprouting and tumour angiogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing CCN1's effects on YAP/TAZ, VEGFR2, DLL4, and tip cell activity.

claim: CCN1 expression induced by activated YAP/TAZ increases tip cell activity in ECs via filopodial formation mediated by the mDia1 Rho effector.
source: Our results indicate that CCN1 expression induced by activated YAP/TAZ increases tip cell activity in ECs via filopodial formation mediated by the mDia1 Rho effector.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: CCN1 increases activation of the VEGFR2, ERK1/2, P38 MAPK, and PI3K signalling pathways by binding with integrin αvβ3 and VEGFR2.
source: CCN1 increases activation of the VEGFR2, ERK1/2, P38 MAPK, and PI3K signalling pathways by binding with integrin αvβ3 and VEGFR2.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings supported by data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: These signalling pathways subsequently induce YAP/TAZ activity and CCN1 expression, sustaining tip cell activity in ECs.
source: These signalling pathways subsequently induce YAP/TAZ activity and CCN1 expression, sustaining tip cell activity in ECs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings illustrated in the model shown in Figure 8.
